title: Out-group Homogeneity Effect
description: We see members of our own group as diverse individuals, but we see members of an out‑group as “all the same.” This strips them of individuality.
shortDescription: We see members of our own group as diverse individuals, but we see members of an out‑group as “all the same.” This strips them of individuality.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We see members of our own group as diverse individuals, but we see members of an out‑group as “all the same.” This strips them of individuality.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A fan of one political party says, “Our side has many different views; theirs is just a bunch of extremists.”
A manager thinks, “Our team is made up of unique people; the other department is just a bunch of slackers.”
An older person says, “Teenagers today are all the same.”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Using broad stereotypes for other groups but nuanced descriptions for your own.
Being surprised when someone from an out‑group doesn’t fit the stereotype.
Assuming you know what an out‑group person thinks without asking.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “He’s not like the others.” (implying “the others” are all identical)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You can describe detailed differences among your friends but only broad categories for people you don’t know.
You assume a whole group shares a single trait because of one or two encounters.
You feel that other groups are predictable while yours is complex.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: We have more contact with our in‑group, so we see their variety. With out‑groups, we lack detailed data, so we rely on a few crude labels. This was documented by Jones, Wood, & Quattrone (1981) and replicated many times.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Actively look for differences within an out‑group. Meet several individuals, not just one.
When you catch yourself thinking “They’re all the same,” ask: “How many have I actually interacted with?”
In cross‑group settings, highlight the diversity within the other group.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking you’re not prejudiced because you “know one who’s different.” That one is treated as an exception, proving the rule.
Assuming all stereotypes are false; some groups have statistical tendencies, but the error is assuming every individual matches the average.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A sales team from Company A considers all competitors’ salespeople as “aggressive and pushy.” When they actually meet several individuals from a rival firm, they’re surprised to find a mix of personalities—one reserved, one funny, one analytical. They had assumed a monolith.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The other side is never a monolith. If you think they are, you haven’t looked closely enough.
